Chapter 7: Building Healthier Relationships – Breaking the Cycle.
You know, our lifetraps show up most clearly in our relationships. That’s where those old patterns seem to come alive—even when we wish they wouldn’t. Breaking out of these cycles isn’t easy, but it’s absolutely possible. It all starts with a bit of self-awareness and a willingness to learn new ways to connect and communicate.
Imagine you’re learning a new dance. It might feel awkward in the beginning, but with practice, it becomes more natural—and a whole lot more enjoyable. This dance is about closeness, honesty, and real respect for each other.
So, what can help you break free from those old, unhelpful patterns? Here are a few guiding principles to keep in mind.
First, recognize your triggers. Pay attention when those familiar feelings—maybe jealousy, fear, or resentment—start bubbling up. Chances are, your lifetrap’s being activated. Instead of reacting right away, take a moment. Pause. Reflect. That small break can make all the difference.
Next, practice open communication. I know, it can feel risky to share what you’re really feeling or needing. But speaking up—using “I” statements—lets you express yourself without putting the other person on the defensive. For example, you might say, “I feel anxious when plans change suddenly, and I need some reassurance.” It’s honest and clear, without blame.
Setting boundaries is another key. Healthy relationships need limits. If you’re used to putting your own needs aside, try saying no, or ask for what you want. And if you find it hard to trust, be upfront about your concerns—and really listen to the other person’s side. Boundaries go both ways.
It also helps to choose supportive people. Surround yourself with those who respect your limits and respond with kindness. Take a step back and notice the patterns in your relationships. Do you gravitate toward people who reinforce your lifetraps, or ones who help you grow?
And remember, everyone makes mistakes. Misunderstandings will happen. What matters is how you repair and forgive. Apologize when you need to, forgive when you can, and always aim for understanding. That’s how trust grows stronger over time.
Let’s look at a real-life example. Imagine someone with an abandonment lifetrap. When their partner is late, anxiety hits hard. Instead of withdrawing or accusing, they might say, “I notice I’m feeling worried, and I’d really appreciate a quick text if you’re running late.” That small shift invites reassurance and connection instead of conflict.
Over time, these new habits start to feel more natural. Relationships become a source of healing, not hurt—and those old lifetraps? They lose their hold on you.
So, if you stick with it, you’ll find that closeness and trust can replace those old cycles. And that’s when relationships truly begin to flourish.
